title: Populorum Progressio (1967)
hookLine: Paul VI: development is the new name for peace

cards: Development is the new name for peace. It sounds like a line off a charity poster. It comes from a papal letter.
Paul the Sixth wrote it near the end of Populorum Progressio, a letter on the development of peoples. The idea underneath fits in a lunch break.
A world where some nations feast while others go hungry is not at peace, however quiet the borders look. If you want peace, the letter says in effect, help people grow. Today's word is that letter.

teach.h: EVERY PERSON, AND THE WHOLE PERSON.
teach.b: First, what development means here. Paul the Sixth insists it can't be measured by money alone. Real development has to promote the good of every person and of the whole person.
Food, yes, and health, and work. But also learning, culture, friendship, prayer. Growth that fills the bank and empties the person isn't what he means.
Second, a hard paragraph about property.
Private property, the letter says, is not an absolute right with no conditions on it. No one may keep for their own exclusive use what they don't need, while others lack what they need to live.
And it calls in a voice from the early Church, Saint Ambrose, who told the wealthy, roughly: when you give to the poor, you aren't giving them what's yours. You're handing back what is theirs.

teach.h: WHAT RICH NATIONS HAVE TO SPARE.
teach.b: The letter asks that what rich countries have beyond their needs be put at the service of poorer ones. Generosity becomes a question for whole peoples. Fourth, peace.

teach.h: THE WORK OF JUSTICE SHALL BE PEACE.
teach.b: Isaiah has a line, in the Douay-Rheims: "And the work of justice shall be peace." Paul the Sixth reads peace the same way. It isn't simply the absence of war.
It gets built, day after day, by justice. That's how a letter about wells, schools and fair trade ends up talking about peace.

how: Catholics often support development work through parish collections and Catholic aid agencies, and Populorum Progressio is a standard text in Catholic teaching on global poverty and fair trade.

o: a Latin hymn for missions in poor lands
the Vatican's yearly report on Church growth
Paul VI's letter on the growth of peoples

p: the work of justice shall be peace

s: the letter measures development by money alone
it asks for the good of every person and of the whole person.
the letter calls private property an absolute right
it says property is not an absolute, unconditioned right.
the letter links development to peace
development, it says, is the new name for peace.

games.q: you have far more than you need, and your neighbor lacks bread. what does Saint Ambrose, quoted in the letter, say giving is?
o: a kind favor you're free to skip.
a reward for those who deserve it.
games.why: Ambrose told the wealthy that giving to the poor is not giving what is yours, but returning what is theirs. Paul VI quoted him.

practice: Bring to mind one kind of work that helps people grow on their own terms: a well dug, a girl kept in school, a small loan for a market stall, a clinic open after dark.
Don't pick the biggest; pick the one that moves you, hold the faces of the people it serves, and ask what you might give it: money, time, a voice. If you pray, hold that work before God.

wordCard.voice: Populorum Progressio. The development of peoples: Paul the Sixth's letter on the growth of every person and the whole person, and on peace built by justice. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: the development, or progress, of peoples, the letter's opening words.

carryVoice: Your line: development is peace. Every person, and the whole person. Same time tomorrow.
